title: Daemon threads: features, use cases, advantages, disadvantages
keyPoints: A daemon thread is a background service thread that does not prevent the JVM from exiting.
The JVM terminates when all non-daemon (user) threads finish, killing daemon threads abruptly.
Call setDaemon(true) before start(); calling it after start() throws IllegalThreadStateException.
Child threads inherit the daemon status of their parent thread.
The garbage collector and JMX threads are daemon threads; the main thread is non-daemon.
Finally blocks in daemon threads may not execute on JVM exit, so do not rely on them for critical cleanup.

s1_definition.oneliner: A daemon thread is a background service thread that does not prevent the JVM from exiting; when all non-daemon threads finish, the JVM terminates and kills all daemon threads abruptly without running their finally blocks.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Daemon thread** – a background thread that does not prevent JVM exit; set via `thread.setDaemon(true)` before `start()`.
- **Non-daemon (user) thread** – a foreground thread that keeps the JVM alive as long as it is running.
- **JVM exit rule** – the JVM terminates when all non-daemon threads finish, killing all daemon threads immediately.
- **Inheritance** – a new thread inherits the daemon status of its parent thread.
- **IllegalThreadStateException** – thrown if `setDaemon()` is called after `start()`.
- **Finally blocks** – may not execute in daemon threads during JVM shutdown, so critical cleanup should use shutdown hooks instead.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, non-daemon threads are the bank tellers serving customers. The bank stays open as long as at least one teller is working. Daemon threads are the cleaning crew working in the background: sweeping floors, restocking forms, refreshing water coolers. When the last teller finishes and goes home, the bank closes immediately. The cleaning crew is kicked out mid-sweep with no chance to finish. Use daemons for background tasks that are safe to abandon.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  JVM Exit Decision

  ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐
  │ User Thread  │     │ User Thread  │     │ Daemon      │
  │ (main)       │     │ (worker-1)   │     │ (GC, cache) │
  └──────┬──────┘     └──────┬──────┘     └──────┬──────┘
         │                    │                    │
         ▼                    ▼                    │
    main() ends         worker finishes            │
         │                    │                    │
         ▼                    ▼                    │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐             │
  │ All user threads finished?       │             │
  │ YES → JVM exits                  │─────────────┘
  │       Daemon threads KILLED      │  (abrupt, no
  │       finally blocks SKIPPED     │   cleanup)
  └──────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A daemon thread is a background service thread that the JVM does not wait for. When all non-daemon (user) threads terminate, the JVM exits immediately, killing all daemon threads without running their finally blocks. The garbage collector, JMX threads, and other JVM internal services are daemon threads.

The rules are straightforward. Call setDaemon(true) before start(). Child threads inherit their parent's daemon status. The main thread is non-daemon. The JVM exit condition is simple: no more non-daemon threads means shutdown.

Use daemon threads for background housekeeping that is safe to abandon: cache refresh, heartbeat monitoring, metrics collection. Use non-daemon threads for critical business logic that must complete: trade settlement, payment processing, data writes. Never put critical cleanup in a finally block inside a daemon thread, because JVM exit can skip it. Use Runtime.addShutdownHook() for critical shutdown logic instead.

At National Bank of India, the cache refresher and heartbeat monitor run as daemon threads. They stop automatically when the trading service shuts down. The log flusher was initially a daemon, but it lost the last five seconds of logs on shutdown. Moving the critical flush to a shutdown hook fixed the problem.

Remember one sentence: daemon threads die when the last user thread exits, so never run critical work on them.
